summary.text: Conservation of momentum says that if a closed system is not affected by outside forces, its total momentum does not change.
The law follows from Newton's laws of motion, holds no matter how complicated the force between particles is, and carries over to relativity in a modified form.
For two interacting particles the forces are equal and opposite, so their momentum changes cancel, and the law expresses translational symmetry of space and time.

items.prompt: A firework bursts into pieces in empty space. Compared with before the burst, what is the pieces' total momentum?

options.label: Larger, from the explosion's energy
The same as before the burst
Smaller, as the pieces scatter
Undefined, since explosions break the law

items.explain: In a closed system the total momentum remains constant, however complicated the forces between the pieces are.

items.prompt: Two skaters at rest in a closed system push apart. Skater A ends with 30 kg⋅m/s of momentum due north. What is skater B's momentum?

options.label: 30 kg⋅m/s due north, matching skater A
Zero, since skater B is only being pushed
15 kg⋅m/s due south, sharing the push
30 kg⋅m/s due south, cancelling skater A's

items.explain: The total momentum stays constant, and it started at zero, so the two momenta must be equal in size and opposite in direction.

items.prompt: Two particles collide and separate. You know both starting momenta and one particle's final momentum. Can you find the other's?

options.label: Yes, the totals before and after must match
No, you must also know the kinetic energy
No, separating particles break the rule
Yes, but only for equal masses

items.explain: The total momentum before equals the total afterwards, so the second particle's momentum is whatever remains.

items.prompt: Five billiard balls in a closed system hit each other in a chain, each pair swapping some momentum. What is the total change in momentum across all the balls?

options.label: It equals the largest single exchange
It grows with each new collision
It adds to zero, so the total stays put
It equals the sum of all the exchanges

items.explain: The momentum exchanged between each pair of particles adds to zero, so the total change in momentum is zero.

items.prompt: A rider on a train moving at steady speed and a person on the platform both track the same collision. Whose bookkeeping shows momentum conserved?

options.label: Only the person on the platform
Only the rider on the train
Neither, since their numbers differ
Both, though they record different totals

items.explain: Momentum depends on the frame, but in each inertial frame the total is conserved.

items.prompt: Momentum conservation is described as expressing which fundamental symmetry of space and time?

options.label: Time-reversal symmetry
Translational symmetry
Rotational symmetry
The constancy of light's speed

items.explain: The law is described as an expression of translational symmetry.

paragraphs.heading: The law in one line
paragraphs.text: Conservation of momentum says that the total momentum of a closed system never changes. A closed system here means one that trades no matter with its surroundings and has no outside forces acting on it. Momentum itself is mass times velocity, p = mv, and it has both a size and a direction.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is true
paragraphs.text: The law follows from Newton's laws of motion. Imagine two particles acting on each other. Newton's third law says those two forces have equal size and point opposite ways. By the second law, each force equals the rate at which that particle's momentum changes, so one particle's momentum rises exactly as fast as the other's falls.

paragraphs.heading: Adding it up
paragraphs.text: Because the two changes cancel, the sum p₁ + p₂ stays fixed, which is written d/dt(p₁ + p₂) = 0. Put in terms of masses and velocities, the total of mass times velocity for the two particles is the same before and after they interact. This works however complicated the force between the particles is.

paragraphs.heading: Many particles at once
paragraphs.text: With more than two particles, the same idea applies to every pair. The momentum swapped within each pair adds to zero, so the total change is zero. Across the whole group, the sum of each mass times its velocity stays constant.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing a viewpoint
paragraphs.text: The value of momentum depends on the frame of reference you measure from. In any inertial frame, though, the total is conserved. And since momentum points in a direction, it helps predict how fast and which way objects move once they collide.

paragraphs.heading: A deep symmetry
paragraphs.text: The law expresses a basic symmetry of space and time known as translational symmetry. It survives, in modified forms, in special relativity, electrodynamics, quantum mechanics, quantum field theory and general relativity. Even fluids and electromagnetic fields have a momentum per unit volume that obeys a conservation law. For fluids, this leads to the Navier–Stokes equations.
